entries.title: Justice Department can no longer pressure Facebook, Apple to remove ICE-sighting apps, judge rules
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge has ordered the Justice Department and U.S. Department of Homeland Security not to pressure Facebook and Apple from banning ICE-monitoring apps and social media groups.</p><p>The preliminary injunction ruling, issued last week by U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso, stems from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/12/chicago-area-resident-lawsuit-facebook-ice-tracking-app" target="_blank" >a lawsuit filed in February by Kassandra “Kae” Rosado</a> against former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi and U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem.</p><p>Rosado alleges that both federal agencies coerced Facebook into removing her “ICE Sighting-Chicagoland” group, which aimed to keep residents informed about where U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were seen in the Chicago area.</p><p>Mark Hodges, an Indiana resident who created the mobile app Eyes Up, which allowed users to record, securely store and view videos of ICE officers committing potential civil rights violations, also joined the lawsuit. The lawsuit claims Apple removed Hodges’ app from the App Store in October — during the height of the Trump administration’s “Operation Midway Blitz” deportation campaign — after pressure from the federal government.</p><p>The judge’s order says Justice Department and DHS officials can no longer take actions to demand or pressure Facebook to suppress Rosado’s Facebook group or pressure Apple to suppress Hodges’ app.</p><p>The Justice Department and DHS were given until Tuesday to notify its employees, Facebook’s parent company Meta, and Apple of the order, and to file a status report documenting the agencies’ actions to comply.</p><p>Rosado’s group had nearly 100,000 members in October and had thousands of posts and comments per day about immigration-related arrests and violent interactions with immigration agents across the Chicago area.</p><p>On Oct. 12, right-wing activist and Trump ally Laura Loomer <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/1977345952718438707" target="_blank" >tagged</a> the Justice Department and DHS leaders in a post claiming that the Facebook page and others like it “are getting people killed.” The next day, Loomer said in a post that a Justice Department source told her that they had contacted executives at Meta, “to tell them they need to remove these ICE tracking pages from the platform.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/31/3c4137a74795885492c17aa7137c/show-temp-14.pdf" target="_blank" ><i>Read the preliminary injunction</i></a><i>:</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/31/3c4137a74795885492c17aa7137c/show-temp-14.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Man’s bid for a retrial in boy’s murder hinges on ex-Chicago cop’s alleged ties to Gitmo torture
entries.summary: <p>A man who says Chicago police beat him into confessing to the 1992 murder of 7-year-old Dantrell Davis is a step closer to finding out whether he’ll get a new trial.</p><p>One of Anthony Garrett’s attorneys battled a Cook County prosecutor in closing arguments Monday afternoon at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p><p>The attorney, Jennifer Blagg, argued that retired Detective Richard Zuley, 79, coordinated her client's torture. She tied the case to alleged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/04/13/settlement-finance-committee-richard-zuley-chicago-detective-carl-reed-coerced-confession" target="_blank" >Zuley-led coercion</a> in a string of cases from 1987 to 2003, including four murder convictions that were later thrown out.</p><p>“He’s never in the room when the worst stuff happens, but he doesn’t have to be [because the officers] are all working together,” Blagg said.</p><p>She also likened Garrett’s case to torture that happened when Zuley was a U.S. Naval reservist at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. She recounted November testimony by Mohamedou Ould Slahi, 55, who appeared via Zoom from Rotterdam, the Dutch city.</p><p>Slahi, a Sept. 11 terror suspect, alleged that Zuley subjected him to months of torture in 2003 at the notorious detention camp at Guantánamo.</p><p>Slahi wrote a memoir about the experience that formed the basis of a 2021 film drama starring Jodie Foster and Benedict Cumberbatch.</p><p>“The real Dick Zuley, I would submit to the court, is the one Mohamedou Ould Slahi saw,” Blagg said Monday.</p><p>But the prosecutor, Armando G. Sandoval, urged Judge Adrienne E. Davis to disregard claims against Zuley in other cases, calling them “allegations, not findings,” and saying they “have no connection to Garrett.”</p><p>“I’m not saying everything Slahi says is false,” Sandoval said. “But the court should be careful of treating the book … or the movie as objective.”</p><p>Sandoval also cast doubt on claims by Garrett that two large men wearing sports jerseys beat him at Zuley’s behest while he was shackled to an eyebolt, and that the two men focused many of their blows on a part of his leg where physicians had implanted a rod after a gunshot wound.</p><p>The prosecutor pointed to testimony that Garrett, after his interrogation, was not limping and did not seem to be injured.</p><p>Sandoval also noted Garrett’s initial claim that the beating took place with a rubber hose. The story changed years later, Sandoval said, when Garrett claimed it was carried out with the hose and a phone book.</p><p>“His account shifts,” Sandoval said. “That’s important.”</p><p>Dantrell was killed on Oct. 13, 1992, as he walked to school with his mother from Cabrini-Green, a former North Side public housing complex. Police said a sniper shot him from an upper floor of a building.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div> </div><p>A jury convicted Garrett in 1994. Now 67, he’s imprisoned at downstate Centralia Correctional Center. He’s not scheduled for release until 2039, according to the Illinois Department of Corrections.</p><p>Monday’s proceedings stem from a 2023 referral by the Illinois Torture and Relief Commission that detailed an “overwhelming” history of “lengthy and consistent” complaints alleging psychological and physical torture involving Zuley. He was hired by CPD in 1970 and worked more than three decades for the department.</p><p>Slahi, who knew Zuley as Capt. Collins, testified the detective led <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/25/mohamedou-ould-slahi-guantanamo-chicago-police-richard-zuley-anthony-garrett-torture-dantrell-davis" target="_blank" >“enhanced interrogation techniques,”</a> including isolation, temperature extremes, beatings, sexual humiliation, sleep deprivation, waterboarding, barking dogs, a mock execution at sea, and round-the-clock mistreatment with strobe lights and a looped recording of the U.S. national anthem.</p><p>After 70 days of torture, Slahi testified, the detective convinced him that U.S. authorities were allowing his mother to be kidnapped and raped. Slahi admitted he never saw Zuley lay a hand on him but added that he wouldn’t know because he was usually blindfolded.</p><p>Slahi testified he eventually confessed to anything his interrogators fed him, starting with plans to attack Toronto’s CN Tower. He said he also falsely confirmed that many individuals had Al Qaeda links.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/08/ex-gitmo-detainee-could-air-allegations-of-torture-by-former-chicago-detective" target="_blank" >Slahi was held at Guantánamo</a> for 14 years without charges before he was released to his native Mauritania in 2016. His memoirs about those years were published as a book that led to the film, “The Mauritanian,” directed by Kevin Macdonald.</p><p>At a November hearing, a prosecutor pressed Slahi about visits to Afghanistan in the early 1990s. Slahi answered he was working for U.S. allies there and cut Al Qaeda ties years before the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/19/ex-chicago-det-richard-zuley-denies-torturing-out-confession-to-7-year-old-dantrell-daviss-murder" target="_blank" >Zuley testified</a> at Feb. 18 and April 1 hearings in Garrett’s case. The former detective said he didn’t know of anyone at the police station handcuffing Garrett to the eyebolt or subjecting him to any physical or mental abuse.</p><p>Zuley testified he left other detectives in charge of Garrett overnight. The next morning, the former detective said, Garrett said he had fired at members of a rival gang near Dantrell. Garrett later signed a handwritten confession.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5aee1be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d4ba8a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1c2a5e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/632x355+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2Ffd%2Fec8693cb405a8749cacc3501ea56%2Fscreenshot-2025-04-07-at-10-18-19-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Anthony Garrett is imprisoned at Centralia Correctional Center. entries.title: Sky face first true playoff-caliber test against Valkyries
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — Beating the Fire in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/09/sky-survive-first-road-test-against-fire" >the regular-season opener </a>was a good sign for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>.</p><p>Sure, the Fire are an expansion franchise that won't sniff the playoffs this season. But you don't scoff at any wins if you're the Sky. Not when you scraped together only 10 of them last year. Not when four of your top eight players were watching in street clothes.</p><p>You can earn a few stripes beating a bad team short-handed.</p><p>But you really earn your "good-team" credentials by beating other good teams.</p><p>The Sky get their shot Wednesday night against the Valkyries. Another sellout crowd, another hostile environment. The first real chance to prove they belong in the playoff conversation.</p><p>Plenty to worry about until then.</p><p>The second half against the Fire flashed a few warning signs. Shooters left wide open in transition. Point guards dribbling the length of the floor without anyone stepping up to stop them.</p><p>At practice Monday, coach Tyler Marsh called it "coverage slippage" that needed to be cleaned up.</p><p>It will need to be squeaky clean against the Valkyries.</p><p>Golden State is well-coached, on a mission, and dangerous at every position. Their backup center, Janelle Salaun, makes it rain from deep in ways most Sky starters don't. Guards Veronica Burton and Gabby Williams make a living getting into the paint.</p><p>"A lot of their offense is based on engaging two," Natasha Cloud told the Sun-Times. "Coming off ball screens, engaging two defenders and they're really great at [making the extra pass]. As much as we can, we've got to guard our yard and take pride in our individual defense so that we're not coming into our secondary and third level of help."</p><p>Having a versatile defender like Cloud back will certainly help. But the Valkyries’ offense challenges the exact two weak points of the Sky's defense last season: containing dribble penetration and defending the arc. Time to show that this year is different.</p><p>Sky players and coaches keep pointing to the athleticism, quickness, and length on the new roster as reasons to believe they can be better defensively. Those are solid ingredients, but they won’t come together without a recipe. Does Marsh have one?</p><p>Wednesday will give us a clue.</p><p>For now, there's enough from the Fire game for Marsh to feel good about.</p><p>The offense looked cohesive. The Skylar Diggins-Kamilla Cardoso pick-and-roll was cooking.</p><p>And when the Sky looked like they were about to throw away a lead — like they did so often last season — they said, no, actually, we're not doing that. Not this time.</p><p>This year, they have Diggins' leadership to fall back on. Someone to step up and hit a big fourth-quarter three — not even her specialty — then throw her head back, stick her tongue out, let the crowd know the party is over.</p><p>The Sky also got a clutch performance from veteran center Elizabeth Williams, who came off the bench to deliver blocks and buckets when it mattered most.</p><p>Those are foundational elements to build on.</p><p>"We got to come with the same level of focus and be able to clean up the areas that we need to, but also stay true to the things that we did well coming out of Portland," Marsh said.</p><p>Clean it up and stay true.
